## Background

This note records a practical lesson about how scientific papers are
found via topic search — written up after running a small empirical
experiment to figure out why a methodologically relevant paper
(León et al. 2024, *Statistics in Medicine*) failed to surface on
broad topic queries about its application dataset (ACTG175) and
core methodological domain (heterogeneous treatment effects).

The experiment is narrow. The lesson generalises.

## The framing question

The right question to ask before a paper is published is *not*
"what is this paper about?" but rather:

> **What query would a reader who has never heard of me, my method,
> or this paper run, and would the paper's title, abstract, and
> keywords match that query well enough to rank in the top ten
> results?**

These are different questions. The first is about content; the
second is about *discoverability*. Discoverability is what determines
whether your paper reaches readers outside its existing citation
neighbourhood.

## The experiment

The setup. León et al. (2024) is the methodology paper for the
`forestsearch` R package. It applies the proposed method to two
public datasets — an oncology trial and the AIDS Clinical Trials
Group Study 175 (ACTG175) HIV trial. ACTG175 is one of the most
heavily reused benchmark datasets in the heterogeneous-treatment-
effect (HTE) and subgroup-identification literatures.

Two topic queries were run, of the kind a reader who had never
heard of `forestsearch` might naturally use:

1. `ACTG175 differential treatment effects`
2. `ACTG175 heterogeneous treatment effects`

Result: the León 2024 paper did not appear in the top ten results
for either query. Several other ACTG175 + HTE papers — Lu/Zhang/
Zeng (2013), Sun et al. (2024), Lee/Ghosh/Yang (2024), Cui et al.
(2023), Johnson/Lu/Davidian (2023), and the Xi/Huang/Wang (2026)
arXiv preprint — surfaced immediately.

A third, name-anchored query was then run as a control:

3. `Leon 2024 forestsearch ACTG175 subgroup consistency bootstrap`

The León paper still did not appear in the top ten, even though the
query contained the author surname, year, package name, dataset
name, and two distinguishing methodological keywords. This rules
out simple keyword failure and points at something structural.

## The empirical finding

Inspecting the paper's title and metadata directly explains both
results. The paper's title is

> *Exploratory subgroup identification in the heterogeneous Cox
> model: A relatively simple procedure*

and the author-supplied keywords are: *bootstrap bias-correction,
censored data, cross-validation, generalized random forests,
virtual twins.* The abstract refers to the application dataset
generically as *"a clinical trial in oncology, and HIV"* and never
uses the string *"ACTG175"* anywhere in the title, abstract, or
keyword list.

This is the structural answer. Search indexers — Google Scholar,
Semantic Scholar, and the index used in this experiment — weight
title, abstract, and author-supplied keywords very heavily, and
weight full text much less. When the dominant token in a query
is a string that never appears in the high-signal fields of a
paper, that paper falls out of the top-ranked results regardless of
how substantively relevant it is.

The papers that *did* surface — Sun et al. (2024), Lee/Ghosh/Yang
(2024), and so on — all explicitly name *ACTG175* in their
abstracts. That single editorial choice is the main difference in
discoverability.

## Two distinct gaps

The experiment surfaced two different failure modes that are easy
to conflate:

**A search-strategy gap on the reader's side.** A reader may anchor
their queries on names and concepts they already know, missing
papers outside that neighbourhood. This is a fixable user-side
behaviour: cast a wide net, vary vocabulary, and read primary
sources before keyword-crawling.

**A discoverability gap on the paper's side.** Even with a
well-constructed topic query, a paper whose title and abstract
do not use the community-standard vocabulary will rank poorly.
This is a fixable author-side property of the paper, but only
*before* publication.

Both gaps stack. Even after a reader corrects their search
strategy, the discoverability gap on the paper's side remains.

## Practical heuristics for future drafts

The following are the takeaways that fall out of the experiment.

### Name your datasets explicitly in the abstract

Public benchmark datasets — ACTG175, GBSG, SPRINT, MERIT-HF, ATLAS,
and so on — are search anchors for the communities that use them.
A paper that applies its method to one of these datasets but refers
to it generically ("an HIV trial", "a breast cancer dataset") is
invisible to anyone searching by dataset name. Putting the exact
dataset name in the abstract once is a single sentence's worth of
revision; the discoverability gain is large.

### Use the vocabulary of the community you want to reach

Many statistical methods sit at the intersection of two
communities that use overlapping but non-identical vocabulary.
The "subgroup identification" community (Lipkovich, Dmitrienko,
SIDES, Foster–Taylor–Ruberg) and the "heterogeneous treatment
effects" community (Athey, Wager, Künzel, X-learner, causal
forests) overlap substantively but search for papers using
different terms. Picking one framing for the title is fine, but
for the abstract and keywords it is worth covering both.

### Treat author-supplied keywords as discoverability real estate

Indexers treat author-supplied keywords as high-signal text
equivalent to title and abstract. A keyword slot used for a
generic methodological term ("censored data", "cross-validation")
that thousands of papers also list is almost wasted. A keyword
slot used for a community-standard search term that
topic-searchers actually type ("heterogeneous treatment effects",
"subgroup identification", "ACTG175") is high-leverage.

### Test your paper against topic search *before* submission

Take three or four topic queries a reader unfamiliar with the
work might run — for example:

- `subgroup identification survival data bootstrap`
- `heterogeneous treatment effects Cox model`
- `exploratory subgroup HIV trial`

— and run them on Google Scholar and Semantic Scholar before
the title and abstract are locked in. If the paper does not
appear in the top ten, there is a discoverability gap that will
not fix itself after publication. This is a five-minute exercise.

### Two-population titles cover both audiences

Titles that name both the methodological contribution and the
application domain — "Subgroup identification with bootstrap
bias correction: an application to ACTG175 and an oncology
trial" — get matched by both methodology-oriented queries and
application-oriented queries. They are slightly less elegant
than purely-methodological titles, but the discoverability
return is substantial.

## The deeper lesson

Scientific publishing has shifted from a world in which readers
found papers by browsing journal tables of contents to a world
in which readers find papers via search engines. The conventions
for titles and abstracts have not fully caught up. Many established
title conventions favour methodological elegance over searchability.

Authors who think explicitly about how their paper will land on
a query — not just how it reads — get materially more uptake.
That is not gaming the system. It is recognising that the index
has become the primary discovery surface, and that the paper has
to perform there to reach readers at all.

## What to remember in 30 seconds

The single sentence is this:

> A paper's discoverability is governed almost entirely by what
> appears in its title, abstract, and keywords — not by what
> appears in the body — and a paper that does not name its
> dataset, its community-standard vocabulary, and its key
> application by their canonical search terms will not be found
> by readers outside its existing citation neighbourhood, no
> matter how strong the work itself is.

## Postscript: how this note came to exist

This note was written up after a back-and-forth in which I
(the AI assistant) was asked to do a literature review of ACTG175
HTE papers and missed León 2024 — which is, ironically, the
methodology paper for the very R package the literature review
was being written for. The user (the package author) initially
asked simply *why* the paper was not found.

The first response treated the question as a meta-question about
search strategy and produced an essay rather than running queries.
The user pushed back, correctly, that the question was empirical
and could be answered by actually running searches. Doing so
revealed the title-and-abstract vocabulary gap documented above.

The lesson for me as the assistant: when asked "why didn't your
search find X", run the search. The answer is empirical, not
philosophical. The lesson for the user, in their own words: think
about how the article would appear in searches. Both lessons are
worth keeping.
